explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The text says it flat out: "So King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom." (2 Chronicles 9:22) Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, wasn't just ahead of the pack. He was ahead of ALL the kings on earth. I'd need a lot more than a quarter to compete with that.

Not quite, friend. The text says, "So King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom." (2 Chronicles 9:22) Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, had more riches than every other king on earth, and wisdom on top of it. No king beat him in either one. That's a whole lot of gold sitting on one throne.

explanations.answer: To hear the wisdom God put in his heart
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. "All the kings of the earth sought an audience with Solomon to hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart." (2 Chronicles 9:23) Kings came from all over the earth just to listen. Picture a king showing up at the door for wisdom. I'd have shown up with a tray of cookies.

explanations.answer: To ask him for help against their enemies
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but the text gives a different reason. The kings came "…to hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart." (2 Chronicles 9:23) Nothing in this verse says they came asking for armies or battle help. They came to listen to the wisdom God gave Solomon, and that's what drew them.

explanations.answer: To trade for the gold from his ships
explanations.explanation: The gold and the ships are in the passage, so I see why you picked it. But the verse says the kings came "…to hear the wisdom that God had put in his heart." (2 Chronicles 9:23) The ships of Tarshish are mentioned two verses earlier (2 Chronicles 9:21), and they're not the reason given for the visits. The kings came for the wisdom, friend.
Right on the money, baker. "Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years." (2 Chronicles 9:30) Forty years is a long time to hold a throne. That's a lot of mornings to be king.

Close, but the text says forty. "Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years." (2 Chronicles 9:30) Solomon had ten more years on the throne than you gave him. Ten more years is a lot of extra mornings.

That's a big reign, friend, but a little too big. The verse says, "Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years." (2 Chronicles 9:30) So it's forty, not fifty. Still a long stretch to sit on an ivory throne.

Yes, baker. "…Solomon rested with his fathers and was buried in the city of his father David." (2 Chronicles 9:31) David was Solomon's father, and Solomon reigned in David's place (1 Chronicles 29:23). All that gold, and the passage ends with a burial. That tells you something big, friend.

Saul was made king at Gilgal (1 Samuel 11:15), but he's not Solomon's father. The verse says Solomon "…was buried in the city of his father David." (2 Chronicles 9:31) David, not Saul. Easy to mix up two names, friend.

Samuel anointed David with oil (1 Samuel 16:13), but he wasn't Solomon's father. The text says Solomon "…was buried in the city of his father David." (2 Chronicles 9:31) So the blank is David. Samuel's a good name to know, friend.
That's the one, baker. "And his son Rehoboam reigned in his place." (2 Chronicles 9:31) Solomon's reign ends, and his son takes the throne. The passage closes on that handoff, friend.

Abijah is a name from later in this book (2 Chronicles 13:1), but he isn't the one here. The verse says, "And his son Rehoboam reigned in his place." (2 Chronicles 9:31) So it's Rehoboam who takes over from Solomon. Keep that name handy, friend.

Shimea was David's son, so that's a family name from the same house (1 Chronicles 3:5). But the text says Solomon's own son took over: "And his son Rehoboam reigned in his place." (2 Chronicles 9:31) Not a brother, a son. The throne went down a generation.
